tips.title: Energy, not matter — and the cork
tips.body: A wave transfers **energy without transferring matter**. The mark for the evidence is separate: a floating cork **bobs up and down but stays in the same place**, so the water is not travelling with the wave.

tips.title: Amplitude starts at the centre line
tips.body: Amplitude is measured from the **undisturbed position** to a peak. A graph question will happily offer you the trough-to-peak distance, which is **twice** the amplitude.

tips.title: One equation is given, one is not
tips.body: $v = f\lambda$ is printed on the AQA equation sheet. $T = \dfrac{1}{f}$ is **not**, so that is the one to learn. Knowing which is which saves time in the exam and in revision.

tips.title: Sound is longitudinal
tips.body: Even though an oscilloscope draws it with peaks and troughs. That trace is a **graph of pressure against time**, not a picture of the air — and the air moves **along** the direction of travel.

tips.title: There and back
tips.body: In the echo method the sound covers the distance **twice**, so $v = \dfrac{2d}{t}$. Forgetting it gives exactly **half** the right answer, which makes it easy to spot and easy to check.

why.matters:
Ripples, sound, light, radio and an earthquake look like five unrelated things. Calling them all **waves** is the claim that they are one thing: a disturbance that carries **energy from place to place without carrying any matter with it**. The cork on a pond bobs and stays put.

The payoff is that one set of measurements — amplitude, wavelength, frequency, period — and one equation, $v = f\lambda$, then describe all of them. Learn it on water in a tray and you have learnt it for the light arriving from a star.

examples.title: Counting the seconds after the lightning
examples.body:
The flash and the bang leave together. Light covers the 1 020 m to you in 3.4 **millionths** of a second; the sound takes the full 3 seconds at 340 m/s. So the gap you count is almost entirely the sound's journey, and three seconds is about a kilometre.

That works because light is nearly **900 000** times faster. It is the same reason the two arrive together when the storm is overhead, and why a distant strike is a flash with no bang at all.

examples.title: The aerial that disappeared from phones
examples.body:
An aerial has to be cut to the wave it is catching — about a **quarter of a wavelength**. Since $\lambda = v \div f$ and radio waves all travel at the same speed, a higher frequency means a shorter aerial.

A car radio at 100 MHz wants 75 cm, so it gets a whip on the wing. A 1990s phone at 900 MHz wanted 8.3 cm, which is exactly the stub that stuck out of the top. Wi-Fi at 2.4 GHz wants 3.1 cm, and that fits inside the lid of a laptop.

examples.title: Why the oven turns the food round
examples.body:
A microwave oven runs at 2.45 GHz, so its waves are 12.2 cm long. They bounce off the metal walls and overlap themselves, which leaves a fixed pattern of hot and cold places **half a wavelength apart** — every 6.1 cm. A 25 cm plate spans about four of them, which is why food that is not moved comes out scalding in patches and frozen between them. The turntable drags every part of the meal through the hot spots in turn.

Take the turntable out, melt a tray of chocolate, and measure the gaps: that experiment gives you the speed of light.

steps.title: What a wave actually carries
steps.body:
A wave **transfers energy** from one place to another **without transferring matter**.

That sentence is the whole idea, and the second half is the part students lose marks on. When a wave crosses a pond, the water does not travel to the far side. When sound crosses a room, the air does not move from the speaker to your ear. **The wave moves; the medium stays where it is.**

**The evidence** is something you can see. Put a floating cork on a pond and send ripples past it: the cork bobs **up and down** in the same place. It does not move towards the shore. The spec asks for exactly this — *describe evidence that, for both ripples on a water surface and sound waves in air, it is the wave and not the water or air itself that travels.*

So for a mark, do not write *the water moves across the pond*. Write **the cork bobs up and down but stays in the same place, so the water is not travelling with the wave**.

steps.title: Transverse and longitudinal
steps.body:
There are **two kinds** of wave, and they differ in **one thing only**: the direction the medium vibrates compared with the direction the wave travels.

**Transverse.** The vibrations are at **right angles** to the direction the wave travels. Ripples on water are transverse, and so is every electromagnetic wave. A transverse wave has **peaks** and **troughs**.

**Longitudinal.** The vibrations are **along the same line** as the direction the wave travels. **Sound in air is longitudinal.** A longitudinal wave has **compressions**, where the particles are squashed together, and **rarefactions**, where they are spread apart.

$$\textbf{transverse: vibration} \perp \textbf{travel} \qquad \textbf{longitudinal: vibration} \parallel \textbf{travel}$$

**Two things worth being careful about:**

- **Sound is longitudinal.** It is the example the exam uses, and it is the one people get wrong because sound is usually *drawn* as a transverse wave on a screen. That drawing is a graph of pressure against time, not a picture of the wave.
- **Longitudinal waves need a medium**, because they work by squashing particles together. That is why **sound cannot travel through a vacuum**. Transverse electromagnetic waves can.

A slinky shows both: push it along its length and you get compressions travelling down it; shake it side to side and you get a transverse wave.

steps.title: The four measurements
steps.body:
Four quantities describe any wave, and each has a precise definition the exam expects.

- **Amplitude** — the **maximum displacement of a point on the wave away from its undisturbed position**. Measured from the middle line to a peak, **not** from trough to peak.
- **Wavelength** (λ, lambda) — the distance from a point on one wave to the **equivalent point on the adjacent wave**. Peak to next peak, or trough to next trough. Measured in **metres**.
- **Frequency** (f) — the **number of waves passing a point each second**. Measured in **hertz (Hz)**.
- **Period** (T) — the time for **one complete wave** to pass a point. Measured in **seconds**.

**Amplitude is the one most often lost.** It is measured from the undisturbed position — the centre line — to a peak. Measuring peak to trough gives **twice** the amplitude.

**Period and frequency are reciprocals:**

$$T = \frac{1}{f}$$

So a wave of **50 Hz** has a period of $1 \div 50 = 0.02$ s. And a wave whose period is 0.02 s has a frequency of $1 \div 0.02 = 50$ Hz. Each undoes the other.

**You must recall this equation.** That matters, because the other wave equation is **given** to you — the next step explains which is which.

steps.title: The wave equation
steps.body:
**All waves obey the same equation**, whatever they are:

$$v = f \lambda$$

- **v** — wave speed, in metres per second, m/s
- **f** — frequency, in hertz, Hz
- **λ** — wavelength, in metres, m

**Wave speed is the speed at which the energy is transferred** through the medium — the speed the wave moves.

**Why it works** is worth a moment, because it makes the equation impossible to forget. If **f** waves pass you each second, and each one is **λ** metres long, then **f × λ** metres of wave go past you every second. Metres per second is a speed. The equation is just counting.

**Which equation is given, and which must be recalled.** This is a real distinction in AQA Physics and it is worth knowing:

- $v = f\lambda$ is **given on the equation sheet**.
- $T = \dfrac{1}{f}$ must be **recalled**.

So the one you have to learn is the short one.

**Rearranging.** With three quantities there are three forms, and you will need all of them:

$$v = f\lambda \qquad f = \frac{v}{\lambda} \qquad \lambda = \frac{v}{f}$$

steps.title: Measuring the speed of a wave
steps.body:
The spec asks you to **describe a method** for two measurements. This is **required practical 8**, and questions on it are common.

**Ripples on water, using a ripple tank.**

1. Set up a ripple tank with a motorised dipper making straight waves, and a lamp above casting shadows of the waves on paper below.
2. **Frequency**: count the number of waves passing a point in a measured time, and divide. Counting 12 waves in 4 seconds gives $12 \div 4 = 3$ Hz.
3. **Wavelength**: the waves move too fast to measure one, so measure **ten** wavelengths on the paper and divide by ten. This reduces the percentage error.
4. **Speed**: $v = f\lambda$.

**Sound in air.**

1. Stand a measured distance from a large flat wall — several tens of metres.
2. Make a sharp sound and start a timer, stopping it when the echo returns.
3. The sound has travelled **there and back**, so the distance is **twice** the distance to the wall.
4. $v = \dfrac{2d}{t}$.

**The two techniques that earn marks in any practical question:**

- **Measure many and divide.** Ten wavelengths, or twenty swings, or thirty waves. The measuring error stays the same size while the quantity gets bigger, so the **percentage** error falls.
- **Repeat and mean.** Human reaction time makes a single timing unreliable, so repeat and take a mean.

**And the factor of two.** In the echo method the sound covers the distance **twice**. Forgetting that halves your answer — and it is the single commonest error in the whole practical.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Energy, not matter — and say the evidence.** *A wave transfers energy without transferring matter* earns one mark. Adding *a floating cork bobs up and down but does not move towards the shore* earns the other, because the spec asks for **evidence**, not just the statement.

**Amplitude is from the centre line.** From the undisturbed position to a peak. Trough to peak is **twice** the amplitude, and a graph question will offer you that number to take.

**Sound is longitudinal even though it is drawn transverse.** An oscilloscope trace of sound looks like a transverse wave, but it is a **graph of pressure against time**, not a picture of the air. The air itself moves back and forth along the direction of travel.

**Which equation is given.** $v = f\lambda$ is on the equation sheet; $T = 1/f$ is not. Knowing which is which tells you what to spend revision time on, and it means you never waste time in the exam trying to recall something already printed.

**Why v = fλ cannot be forgotten.** *f* waves pass each second, each *λ* metres long, so *fλ* metres pass each second. The equation is counting metres per second. Reconstructed like that, it survives exam nerves better than a memorised formula.

**What changes and what does not when a wave crosses a boundary.** This is the physics-only extension, and it is neat. When sound passes from one medium into another, the **frequency stays the same** — it is set by the source, and the waves cannot pile up or disappear at the boundary. So if the **speed** changes, the **wavelength** must change with it, because $v = f\lambda$ and *f* is fixed. Sound speeds up going from air into water, so its wavelength gets **longer**. That single argument — *frequency is fixed by the source, so speed and wavelength change together* — answers every question of this kind.

**Ten wavelengths, not one.** The measuring error on a ruler is about the same however much you measure, so measuring a bigger quantity makes the **percentage** error smaller. It is the same reasoning as timing twenty swings of a pendulum instead of one.

**The factor of two in the echo method.** The sound travels to the wall **and back**. Forgetting it does not produce a slightly wrong answer; it produces exactly **half** the right one, which is why it is easy for an examiner to spot and easy for you to check.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- A wave transfers **energy without transferring matter**.
- The **evidence**: a floating cork **bobs up and down** but does not travel to the shore.
- **Transverse**: vibration at **right angles** to travel. Peaks and troughs. Water ripples, all electromagnetic waves.
- **Longitudinal**: vibration **along** the direction of travel. Compressions and rarefactions. **Sound in air.**
- Longitudinal waves **need a medium**, so sound cannot cross a vacuum.
- **Amplitude**: maximum displacement from the **undisturbed position** — not trough to peak.
- **Wavelength** (λ): a point to the **equivalent point** on the next wave, in metres.
- **Frequency** (f): waves passing a point **each second**, in hertz.
- **Period** (T): the time for **one** wave to pass, in seconds.
- $T = \dfrac{1}{f}$ — and you must **recall** this one.
- $v = f\lambda$ — **given** on the equation sheet.
- Rearranged: $f = \dfrac{v}{\lambda}$ and $\lambda = \dfrac{v}{f}$.
- **Ripple tank**: count waves for **f**, measure **ten** wavelengths and divide for λ, then $v = f\lambda$.
- **Echo method**: $v = \dfrac{2d}{t}$ — the sound goes **there and back**.
- **Measure many and divide** to cut the percentage error; **repeat and take a mean**.
- Crossing a boundary, **frequency is fixed by the source**, so speed and wavelength change together.

questions.prompt: Describe a method to measure the speed of ripples on a water surface. Include how you would reduce the uncertainty in your measurements.
questions.solution: Set up a ripple tank containing a shallow depth of water, with a motorised dipper at one end producing straight waves of constant frequency, and a lamp mounted above the tank so that the waves cast shadows on a sheet of white paper beneath it. To find the frequency, count the number of waves passing a fixed point on the paper during a measured time, for example counting twelve waves in four seconds, and divide the count by the time to give a frequency of three hertz. Counting over several seconds rather than timing a single wave reduces the percentage uncertainty, and the count should be repeated and a mean taken because human reaction time makes any single measurement unreliable. To find the wavelength, measure the distance across ten wavelengths on the paper and divide by ten. This is done because the uncertainty in reading the ruler is roughly the same however long the distance measured, so measuring a larger distance makes that uncertainty a smaller fraction of the result. If ten wavelengths measure forty centimetres then one wavelength is four centimetres, which must be converted to metres, giving 0.04 metres. Finally calculate the speed using the wave equation, so that the speed equals the frequency multiplied by the wavelength, three hertz times 0.04 metres, giving 0.12 metres per second.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Apparatus.** A ripple tank with shallow water, a **motorised dipper** making straight waves at a constant frequency, and a **lamp above** casting shadows of the waves onto white paper below.

**Frequency.** Count the waves passing a fixed point in a measured time and divide. Twelve waves in four seconds gives $12 \div 4 = 3$ Hz. Counting over several seconds, and repeating for a mean, reduces the effect of reaction time.

**Wavelength.** Measure **ten** wavelengths and divide by ten. The ruler's uncertainty is roughly fixed, so measuring a larger distance makes it a **smaller fraction** of the result. Ten wavelengths of 40 cm gives one of 4 cm — **0.04 m** once converted.

**Speed.** $v = f\lambda = 3 \times 0.04 = 0.12$ m/s.

**The two marks most often lost** are forgetting to convert centimetres to metres, and measuring a single wavelength instead of ten.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between transverse and longitudinal waves, and explain why this difference means sound cannot travel through a vacuum.
questions.solution: Transverse and longitudinal waves differ in the direction in which the medium vibrates compared with the direction in which the wave travels. In a transverse wave the vibrations are at right angles to the direction of travel, and the wave shows peaks and troughs. Ripples on the surface of water are transverse, and so are all electromagnetic waves, including light and radio waves. In a longitudinal wave the vibrations are along the same line as the direction of travel, and instead of peaks and troughs the wave shows compressions, where the particles of the medium are pushed close together, and rarefactions, where they are spread further apart. Sound travelling through air is longitudinal. This difference explains why sound cannot travel through a vacuum. A longitudinal wave works by particles being squashed together and then spread apart, each particle pushing on the next and so passing the disturbance along. A vacuum contains no particles, so there is nothing to compress and nothing to pass the disturbance on, and the sound cannot propagate. Electromagnetic waves are transverse and consist of oscillating electric and magnetic fields rather than the movement of particles, so they require no medium and can travel through the vacuum of space. This is why we can see the Sun but cannot hear it. It is worth noting that sound is often drawn as a curve with peaks and troughs on an oscilloscope, but that trace is a graph of pressure against time rather than a picture of the wave, and sound remains longitudinal.

questions.modelAnswer:
**The difference is the direction of vibration relative to travel.**

- **Transverse**: vibrations at **right angles** to the direction of travel. **Peaks and troughs.** Water ripples, and all electromagnetic waves.
- **Longitudinal**: vibrations **along** the direction of travel. **Compressions and rarefactions.** Sound in air.

**Why a vacuum stops sound.** A longitudinal wave works by particles being **squashed together and spread apart**, each pushing on the next. A vacuum has **no particles**, so there is nothing to compress and nothing to pass the disturbance along.

**The contrast that earns the last mark.** Electromagnetic waves are transverse and consist of **oscillating electric and magnetic fields**, not moving particles, so they need no medium at all. Which is why we can **see** the Sun but not **hear** it.

**And a caution worth adding:** an oscilloscope draws sound with peaks and troughs, but that is a **graph of pressure against time**, not a picture of the wave. Sound is still longitudinal.

questions.prompt: A student says that because the water in a pond moves towards the shore when waves arrive, waves must transfer matter. Explain why the student is wrong, and describe evidence that would show it.
questions.solution: The student has confused the movement of the wave with the movement of the water. A wave transfers energy from one place to another without transferring matter, and although the wave pattern clearly moves towards the shore, the water itself does not travel with it. Each part of the water surface oscillates about its own undisturbed position as the wave passes through it and then returns to where it started. The evidence for this is straightforward to observe. If a small floating object such as a cork is placed on the surface of the pond and ripples are sent past it, the cork bobs up and down as each wave passes but stays in essentially the same place and is not carried to the shore. If the water were genuinely travelling towards the shore, the cork would travel with it. The same point applies to sound waves in air. When someone speaks across a room the air itself does not move from the speaker to the listener, since if it did there would be a noticeable draught, and only the disturbance passes through the air. What the student may be observing at a real shoreline is that waves break in shallow water, which does move water up the beach, but that is an additional effect and not what the wave itself is doing.

questions.modelAnswer:
**The confusion** is between the movement of the **wave** and the movement of the **water**. The wave pattern travels towards the shore; the water does not travel with it. Each part of the surface **oscillates about its own undisturbed position** and returns to where it started.

**The evidence.** Float a **cork** on the surface and send ripples past it. The cork **bobs up and down but stays in the same place**. If the water were travelling shorewards, the cork would go with it.

**A second example.** When someone speaks across a room, the air does not travel from speaker to listener — if it did there would be a **draught**. Only the disturbance passes through.

**What the student may really be seeing** is waves **breaking** in shallow water, which does carry water up the beach. That is an extra effect of the shallows, not what the wave itself does — and noticing it is what separates a good answer from a full one.

examTechnique.body:
State that a wave transfers energy without transferring matter, and give the cork as evidence when evidence is asked for.

Measure amplitude from the undisturbed position, not from trough to peak.

Recall T = 1/f, and expect v = f lambda to be printed on the equation sheet.

Convert centimetres to metres before substituting into the wave equation.

In the echo method, double the distance because the sound travels there and back.

Measure ten wavelengths and divide by ten, and say that this reduces the percentage uncertainty.

When a wave crosses a boundary, say that the frequency is fixed by the source, so the speed and wavelength change together.
examinerErrors: Writing that the water moves across the pond.
Measuring amplitude from trough to peak, which is twice its value.
Calling sound transverse because an oscilloscope draws it that way.
Forgetting to convert centimetres to metres before using v = f lambda.
Using the one-way distance in the echo method, halving the answer.
Measuring a single wavelength in the ripple tank instead of ten.
Saying the frequency changes when a wave enters a new medium.
Giving a speed with no unit, or with the wrong unit.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer separates the motion of the wave from the motion of the medium, and offers the cork as evidence without being asked twice. It knows amplitude is measured from the centre line and treats a trough-to-peak reading as a trap rather than an answer. It reconstructs v = f lambda by counting metres per second rather than recalling it, and knows that the equation is printed anyway while T = 1/f is not. Faced with a wave crossing a boundary it reasons from the source: the frequency is fixed, so if the speed changes the wavelength must change with it.
